## Implement Queue {#interview-design-queue}

### Problem Metadata

- **Platform**: Interview Prep
- **Problem ID**: Queue Design
- **Difficulty**: Easy
- **URL**: N/A
- **Tags**: `Array`, `Linked List`, `Stack`
- **Techniques**: [Array](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-array), [Linked List](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-linked-list), [Stack](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-stack)

### Description

Implement a queue with operations `enqueue`, `dequeue`, `peek`, and `isEmpty`. Explore multiple representations.

### Examples

```
MyQueue queue = new MyQueue(3);
queue.enqueue(1);
queue.enqueue(2);
queue.dequeue(); // 1
queue.enqueue(3);
queue.peek(); // 2
```

### Constraints

- Assume integers, bounded or unbounded based on implementation

### Solution 1 - Circular Array

#### Walkthrough

Use a fixed-size array with `head`, `tail`, and `count`. Enqueue writes at `tail` then wraps around; dequeue reads from `head`. This avoids shifting elements.

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**: O(1)
- **Space Complexity**: O(capacity)

#### Implementation Steps


1. Initialize `head = 0`, `tail = 0`, `count = 0`.
2. `enqueue(x)`: if count == capacity throw overflow; assign `data[tail] = x`, `tail = (tail + 1) % capacity`, increment count.
3. `dequeue()`: if empty throw, read `data[head]`, advance head, decrement count.
4. `peek()` returns `data[head]`.

#### Java Code

```java
class ArrayQueue {
    private final int[] data;
    private int head = 0;
    private int tail = 0;
    private int count = 0;

    public ArrayQueue(int capacity) {
        this.data = new int[capacity];
    }

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        if (count == data.length) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Queue full");
        }
        data[tail] = x;
        tail = (tail + 1) % data.length;
        count++;
    }

    public int dequeue() {
        if (count == 0) {
            throw new NoSuchElementException();
        }
        int value = data[head];
        head = (head + 1) % data.length;
        count--;
        return value;
    }

    public int peek() {
        if (count == 0) {
            throw new NoSuchElementException();
        }
        return data[head];
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return count == 0;
    }
}
```

### Solution 2 - Linked List

#### Walkthrough

Maintain `front` and `rear` pointers of a singly linked lc-list. Enqueue appends at the tail; dequeue removes from the head.

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**: O(1)
- **Space Complexity**: O(n)

#### Implementation Steps


1. Each node holds value plus `next`.
2. `enqueue(x)`: create node, append at `rear`, update pointers.
3. `dequeue()`: remove `front`, adjusting `rear` when queue becomes empty.

#### Java Code

```java
class LinkedQueue {
    private static class Node {
        int val;
        Node next;
        Node(int val) { this.val = val; }
    }
    private Node front;
    private Node rear;

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        Node node = new Node(x);
        if (rear == null) {
            front = rear = node;
        } else {
            rear.next = node;
            rear = node;
        }
    }

    public int dequeue() {
        if (front == null) {
            throw new NoSuchElementException();
        }
        int value = front.val;
        front = front.next;
        if (front == null) {
            rear = null;
        }
        return value;
    }

    public int peek() {
        if (front == null) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return front.val;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return front == null;
    }
}
```

### Solution 3 - Two Stacks

#### Walkthrough

Use two stacks `in` and `out`. Enqueue pushes onto `in`. Dequeue/peek pop from `out`, reloading it from `in` when empty by moving all elements to reverse order.

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**: Amortized O(1)
- **Space Complexity**: O(n)

#### Implementation Steps


1. `enqueue(x)`: push onto `in`.
2. `dequeue()` / `peek()`: if `out` empty, move all elements from `in` to `out`, then pop/peek.
3. `isEmpty()`: true when `in` and `out` are empty.

#### Java Code

```java
class QueueWithStacks {
    private final Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Integer> out = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        in.push(x);
    }

    public int dequeue() {
        shift();
        return out.pop();
    }

    public int peek() {
        shift();
        return out.peek();
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty();
    }

    private void shift() {
        if (out.isEmpty()) {
            while (!in.isEmpty()) {
                out.push(in.pop());
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Implement Stack Using Queues {#interview-design-stack}

### Problem Metadata

- **Platform**: Interview Prep
- **Problem ID**: Stack via Queue
- **Difficulty**: Easy
- **URL**: N/A
- **Tags**: `Queue`, `Stack`, `Design`
- **Techniques**: [Queue](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-queue)

### Description

Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top`, and `empty` using only standard queue operations.

### Examples

```
MyStack stack = new MyStack();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
stack.top(); // 2
stack.pop(); // 2
stack.empty(); // false
```

### Constraints

- Use only queue operations: enqueue, dequeue, size, isEmpty

### Solution - Single Queue Rotation

#### Walkthrough

Maintain a single queue. For `push(x)` enqueue `x`, then rotate the previous elements to the back by dequeuing and enqueuing `size - 1` times, so that `x` becomes the front. `pop` and `top` are queue front operations.

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**: `push` O(n), others O(1)
- **Space Complexity**: O(n)

#### Implementation Steps


1. `push(x)`: enqueue `x`, then loop `size-1` times moving front to back.
2. `pop()`: dequeue front.
3. `top()`: peek front.
4. `empty()`: check queue emptiness.

#### Java Code

```java
class MyStack {
    private final Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();

    public void push(int x) {
        queue.offer(x);
        for (int i = 0; i < queue.size() - 1; i++) {
            queue.offer(queue.poll());
        }
    }

    public int pop() {
        return queue.poll();
    }

    public int top() {
        return queue.peek();
    }

    public boolean empty() {
        return queue.isEmpty();
    }
}
```

## Time-Based Key-Value Cache {#interview-oracle-time-cache}

### Problem Metadata

- **Platform**: Interview
- **Problem ID**: Oracle Time Cache
- **Difficulty**: Medium
- **URL**: N/A
- **Tags**: `Oracle`, `Hash Table`, `Binary Search`, `Design`
- **Techniques**: [Hash Table](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-hash-table), [Binary Search](glossary-of-algorithm.html#glossary-binary-search)

### Description

Design a cache system that stores key-value pairs with timestamps. Each key can have multiple values associated with different timestamps. The system should support:

1. `void set(String key, int timestamp, String value)`: Store a value for a given key at a specific timestamp
2. `String get(String key, int timestamp)`: Retrieve the most chronologically recent value for the key at or before the given timestamp. Return "" if key is not found
3. `String get(String key)`: Retrieve the most recent (latest timestamp) value for the key

### Examples

```
TimeCache cache = new TimeCache();
cache.set("foo", 1, "bar1");
cache.set("foo", 3, "bar2");
cache.set("foo", 5, "bar3");

cache.get("foo", 2);  // "bar1" (most recent value at or before timestamp 2)
cache.get("foo", 3);  // "bar2" (exact match at timestamp 3)
cache.get("foo", 4);  // "bar2" (most recent value at or before timestamp 4)
cache.get("foo");     // "bar3" (latest value)
cache.get("baz", 10); // null (key does not exist)
```

### Constraints

- Timestamps are non-negative integers
- Multiple `set` operations with the same key but different timestamps should maintain chronological order
- `get` with timestamp should return "" if no value exists at or before that timestamp
- `get` without timestamp should return "" if key does not exist

### Solution - Hash Map with Sorted List

#### Walkthrough

Use a `HashMap<String, List<Entry>>` where each key maps to a list of `(timestamp, value)` entries sorted by timestamp. The outer HashMap provides O(1) key lookups, while the inner sorted list enables binary search for timestamp queries.

For `set(key, timestamp, value)`:
1. Retrieve or create the entry list for the key
2. Add the new entry to the list
3. Sort the entire list by timestamp to maintain chronological order
4. Store the updated list back in the cache

For `get(key, timestamp)`:
1. Retrieve the entry list (return empty string if key doesn't exist)
2. Use `Collections.binarySearch()` to find the target timestamp
3. If exact match found (result $\ge$ 0), return that value
4. If no exact match (result $\lt$ 0), convert to insertion point using `insertionPoint = -result - 1`
5. Return the entry at `insertionPoint - 1` (the most recent entry before the timestamp)
6. If insertionPoint is 0, no entry exists at or before the timestamp, return empty string

For `get(key)`:
- Simply return the last element in the sorted list (most recent timestamp)
- Return empty string if key doesn't exist

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**:
  - `set`: O(n log n) due to sorting the entire list on each insert
  - `get(key, timestamp)`: O(log n) with binary search
  - `get(key)`: O(1) - direct access to last element
- **Space Complexity**: O(k × m) where k is number of unique keys and m is average entries per key

**Key Insight**: The critical logic is handling `Collections.binarySearch()` return values. When the timestamp is not found, the return value is `-(insertion point) - 1`. We need the entry just before this insertion point to get the most recent value at or before the queried timestamp.

**Optimization Opportunities**:
1. Current `set` sorts on every insert (O(n log n)). If timestamps are guaranteed to arrive in order, we could append directly (O(1)). Otherwise, binary search for insertion point reduces to O(n) due to array shifting.
2. Alternative: Use `TreeMap<Integer, String>` per key instead of sorted list. This would make `set` O(log n) and enable `floorEntry()` for efficient "at or before" queries.

#### Implementation Steps

1. Define an `Entry` class holding `timestamp` and `value`
2. Maintain `Map<String, List<Entry>>` to store entries per key
3. For `set(key, timestamp, value)`: retrieve or create list, add entry, sort by timestamp, store back
4. For `get(key, timestamp)`: retrieve list, binary search for timestamp, handle exact match vs insertion point cases
5. For `get(key)`: retrieve list, return last entry's value

#### Java Code

```java
class TimeCache {
    private static class Entry {
        int timestamp;
        String value;
        Entry(int timestamp, String value) {
            this.timestamp = timestamp;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, List<Entry>> cache = new HashMap<>();

    public void set(String key, int timestamp, String value) {
        List<Entry> entries = cache.getOrDefault(key, new ArrayList<>());

        Entry entry = new Entry(timestamp, value);
        entries.add(entry);

        Collections.sort(entries, new Comparator<Entry>() {
            @Override
            public int compare(Entry e1, Entry e2) {
                return Integer.compare(e1.timestamp, e2.timestamp);
            }
        });

        cache.put(key, entries);
    }

    public String get(String key, int timestamp) {
        List<Entry> entries = cache.getOrDefault(key, new ArrayList<>());
        if (entries.isEmpty()) {
            return "";
        }

        int result = Collections.binarySearch(entries, new Entry(timestamp, ""),
            new Comparator<Entry>() {
                @Override
                public int compare(Entry e1, Entry e2) {
                    return Integer.compare(e1.timestamp, e2.timestamp);
                }
            });

        if (result >= 0) {
            return entries.get(result).value;
        } else {
            int insertionPoint = -result - 1;
            if (insertionPoint == 0) {
                return "";
            }
            return entries.get(insertionPoint - 1).value;
        }
    }

    public String get(String key) {
        List<Entry> entries = cache.getOrDefault(key, new ArrayList<>());
        if (entries.isEmpty()) {
            return "";
        }
        return entries.get(entries.size() - 1).value;
    }
}
```

### Solution 2 - Hash Map with TreeMap

#### Walkthrough

Use a `HashMap<String, TreeMap<Integer, String>>` where each key maps to a TreeMap with timestamps as keys and values as map values. TreeMap maintains sorted order automatically and provides `floorEntry()` to find the largest timestamp not exceeding the query.

For `set(key, timestamp, value)`:
- Simply `cache.get(key).put(timestamp, value)` - TreeMap handles ordering

For `get(key, timestamp)`:
- Use `floorEntry(timestamp)` to get the entry with the largest timestamp $\le$ query timestamp
- Return the value from the entry, or empty string if null

For `get(key)`:
- Use `lastEntry()` to get the entry with the maximum timestamp
- Return its value, or empty string if null

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**:
  - `set`: O(log n) - TreeMap insertion
  - `get(key, timestamp)`: O(log n) - TreeMap floorEntry lookup
  - `get(key)`: O(log n) - TreeMap lastEntry lookup
- **Space Complexity**: O(k × m) where k is number of unique keys and m is average entries per key

**Trade-offs vs Solution 1**:
- **Pros**: Cleaner code, better `set` performance (O(log n) vs O(n log n)), built-in sorted order
- **Cons**: Slightly higher constant factors, more memory overhead per entry
- **Best for**: Production systems where code maintainability and consistent performance matter

#### Implementation Steps

1. Maintain `Map<String, TreeMap<Integer, String>>` to store entries per key
2. For `set(key, timestamp, value)`: get or create TreeMap for key, put timestamp-value pair
3. For `get(key, timestamp)`: use `floorEntry()` to find largest timestamp not exceeding query
4. For `get(key)`: use `lastEntry()` to get most recent entry

#### Java Code

```java
class TimeCacheTreeMap {
    private final Map<String, TreeMap<Integer, String>> cache = new HashMap<>();

    public void set(String key, int timestamp, String value) {
        cache.putIfAbsent(key, new TreeMap<>());
        cache.get(key).put(timestamp, value);
    }

    public String get(String key, int timestamp) {
        TreeMap<Integer, String> entries = cache.get(key);
        if (entries == null) {
            return "";
        }

        Map.Entry<Integer, String> entry = entries.floorEntry(timestamp);
        return entry == null ? "" : entry.getValue();
    }

    public String get(String key) {
        TreeMap<Integer, String> entries = cache.get(key);
        if (entries == null || entries.isEmpty()) {
            return "";
        }

        return entries.lastEntry().getValue();
    }
}
```

### Solution 3 - Optimized Binary Insertion

#### Walkthrough

Similar to Solution 1 but avoids sorting on every insert. Instead, use binary search to find the correct insertion position and insert at that index, maintaining sorted order incrementally.

For `set(key, timestamp, value)`:
1. Retrieve or create entry list for the key
2. Binary search for insertion point
3. Insert at the correct position to maintain sorted order

This reduces `set` from O(n log n) to O(n) while keeping the same query performance.

#### Analysis

- **Time Complexity**:
  - `set`: O(n) - binary search O(log n) + ArrayList insertion O(n)
  - `get(key, timestamp)`: O(log n) - binary search
  - `get(key)`: O(1)
- **Space Complexity**: O(k × m)

**Trade-offs vs Solution 1 and 2**:
- **Pros**: Better than sorting (O(n) vs O(n log n)), uses familiar ArrayList
- **Cons**: Still O(n) for insert due to array shifting, more complex than TreeMap
- **Best for**: When timestamps arrive mostly in order but occasional out-of-order inserts occur

#### Implementation Steps

1. Define an `Entry` class holding `timestamp` and `value`
2. Maintain `Map<String, List<Entry>>` to store entries per key
3. For `set`: binary search for insertion point, insert at that position
4. For `get(key, timestamp)`: binary search as in Solution 1
5. For `get(key)`: return last entry

#### Java Code

```java
class TimeCacheBinaryInsert {
    private static class Entry {
        int timestamp;
        String value;
        Entry(int timestamp, String value) {
            this.timestamp = timestamp;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    private static final Comparator<Entry> COMPARATOR =
        (e1, e2) -> Integer.compare(e1.timestamp, e2.timestamp);

    private final Map<String, List<Entry>> cache = new HashMap<>();

    public void set(String key, int timestamp, String value) {
        cache.putIfAbsent(key, new ArrayList<>());
        List<Entry> entries = cache.get(key);

        Entry entry = new Entry(timestamp, value);
        int pos = Collections.binarySearch(entries, entry, COMPARATOR);

        if (pos < 0) {
            pos = -pos - 1;
        }

        entries.add(pos, entry);
    }

    public String get(String key, int timestamp) {
        List<Entry> entries = cache.get(key);
        if (entries == null || entries.isEmpty()) {
            return "";
        }

        int result = Collections.binarySearch(entries, new Entry(timestamp, ""), COMPARATOR);

        if (result >= 0) {
            return entries.get(result).value;
        } else {
            int insertionPoint = -result - 1;
            if (insertionPoint == 0) {
                return "";
            }
            return entries.get(insertionPoint - 1).value;
        }
    }

    public String get(String key) {
        List<Entry> entries = cache.get(key);
        if (entries == null || entries.isEmpty()) {
            return "";
        }
        return entries.get(entries.size() - 1).value;
    }
}
```
